Enter a whole number of seconds from %1$d to %2$d. The timeout stays at %3$d until you do.

Scripts in a project\'s .codeonthego/hooks folder run only after you read and trust them in the Hooks tab, because a script can arrive with a project: a cloned repository, or an AI agent\'s edit. Only plain scripts can be trusted: printable ASCII and newlines, no tabs, no line over 100 characters or ending in a space, at most 64 KB. They need no executable bit.

". It runs with the same access as the Terminal, including the network. Each numbered row below is one line of the script, and a row marked ↳ continues the line above it. You see every character, but reviewing is reading code: read it as the shell will. Watch for three things. A backslash at the end of a line of code joins the next line to it, so a # starting that line does not begin a comment; at the end of a comment, a backslash does nothing. A here-document ends at the first line that exactly matches its delimiter, which may not be the line you expect. And backticks or $( in here-document text run commands unless the delimiter is quoted. Trust covers only this script: not other project files it runs, and not settings that tools read by themselves, such as hooks in .git/config (core.fsmonitor runs a program on git status) or the project\'s Gradle and npm files. Trust it only if you have read it and know what it does."

Best-effort check, not a guarantee. Lines that use the syntax below are marked ! beside their numbers, wherever it appears, comments and strings included. A line without a mark can still do anything, so read every line.

Lines with <<: %1$s. Each may start a here-document. Find the line that ends it, and check whether its text is expanded: unless the word after << is quoted, $ in the text is expanded, and backticks and $( in it run commands.

Lines ending in a backslash: %1$s. In code, the shell joins the next line to such a line, so a # starting the next line does not begin a comment. At the end of a comment the backslash does nothing, and the next line is a command of its own.
Lines with a backtick or $(: %1$s. Each may run a command, even inside double quotes or here-document text.

resources.string: Line %1$d, marked for a check above

Can\'t be reviewed: %1$s. A project script can be trusted only if it is plain: printable ASCII and newlines, no tabs or carriage returns, no line over 100 characters or ending in a space, at most 64 KB, and a name of letters, digits, \'.\', \'_\', \'-\' and \'/\' with no part starting with \'.\'. Anything else could look different here from how it runs, so it never runs.
